title: A detonation running down a closed tube of hydrogen and air

outcome.label: Completed, with differences from what was expected

goal: Shock and burning together for the first time. Step 4 of 7 on the way to a rotating detonation engine.
story: Solved with OpenFOAM's burning solver by a fresh agent. gpucfd's shock solver and its chemistry were joined afterwards and run on the same tube. That showed a weakness of the case itself: with cells finer than OpenFOAM's study used, the detonation never starts.

requirements: A closed tube, 0.12 m long, of hydrogen and air at rest at 1 atmosphere and \(300\,\mathrm{K}\). Only the distance along the tube matters.
A thin layer at one end (1.5 mm) starts hot and at high pressure. It is meant to send a shock down the tube that ignites the gas behind it: a detonation.
The full hydrogen reaction scheme: 10 species and 27 reactions.
Asked for: the speed of the wave, whether shock and flame travel together, the burnt gas behind the wave, the peak pressure at the front, whether mass, atoms and energy are kept, and the cost.
Reference: the Chapman-Jouguet speed, the one speed a free-running detonation can have. It follows from the gas alone, with no simulation.
Required: wave speed within 2 % of that theory; from 10 microseconds on, the flame within 1 mm of the shock.

results.headline: Completed, with one difference from what was expected. OpenFOAM's reactingFoam carries a detonation down the tube at \(1968.4\,\mathrm{m/s}\), \(0.51\,\%\) below the Chapman-Jouguet speed (required: within \(2\,\%\)), with the burning front \(0.06\,\mathrm{mm}\) or less behind the pressure front (required: within \(1\,\mathrm{mm}\)). gpucfd's joined solver, built after this case was solved, runs the same tube on the same grids. On 3200 cells its wave travels at \(1968.3\,\mathrm{m/s}\) (-0.52 % from the theory), with the burning front \(0.06\,\mathrm{mm}\) behind the pressure front, in 6 s on the GPU against 401 s on 8 cores, and it keeps mass and energy to rounding. On finer grids (4000 cells and more) gpucfd finds no detonation at all: the hot layer of the problem is too weak to ignite the gas behind its own shock, and on coarser cells it is the smearing of the scheme that holds shock and flame together. OpenFOAM was not run on such grids.
meaning: Both tools meet both requirements with a wide margin on every grid of OpenFOAM's study, the coarsest included. The speed is right even where the front is not resolved, because it follows from keeping mass, momentum and energy and burning the gas completely.

A weakness of the case: the hot layer cannot start a detonation by its shock. That shock heats the gas to about \(930\,\mathrm{K}\), and such gas needs over 200 microseconds to ignite; the run lasts 50. On coarse cells the scheme smears hot burnt gas into the fresh gas, and that starts the wave.
Once started, the wave is a real detonation: the two tools agree on its speed and on the burnt gas behind it. gpucfd keeps mass, atoms and energy to rounding; OpenFOAM lost 0.2 % of the heat.

For the detonation engine: OpenFOAM's solver does not keep energy by itself. With the setting of its own burning examples it lost 15 % of the heat and the wave ran 17 % too slow. Five passes per time step cut the loss to 0.2 %, at five times the cost.

One prediction of the agent was missed by a hair: the peak pressure at the front reaches 0.79 of the full shock pressure on the finest grid, where it expected at least 0.80. The burning zone is thinner than the cells.
With the GPU full (the same tube in 1024 rows, 1.2 million cells), gpucfd needs 49 nanoseconds for a cell and a time step. OpenFOAM needed about 19 000 on 8 cores.
limits: The answer depends on the cell size: a detonation with up to 3200 cells, none with 4000 or more (gpucfd). OpenFOAM's study stopped at 3200 cells and was not run finer.

A trial with gpucfd on a tube four times longer with a stronger ignition (not this case's problem): on cells of 100 to 25 micrometres the wave settles 0.3 % above the theoretical speed, the same on the three grids. On cells of 12.5 and 6.25 micrometres the detonation dies on the way. Whether a detonation in one dimension survives on such fine cells is open.
The times are not like for like: one GPU against 8 cores, different time steps, different chemistry settings, and gpucfd in mixed precision.
The time-step study of OpenFOAM shows no trend and three small effects stay unexplained.
The reference is a theory value from the scheme's own data. Values in the literature for this mixture may differ by about half a per cent; none was checked.
answer: OpenFOAM carries the detonation down the tube at the theoretical speed to within about half a per cent. 2 % was allowed.
gpucfd, joined afterwards, gives the same wave speed on the same grid. It needs 6 seconds on the GPU, where OpenFOAM needed 401 seconds on 8 cores.
In both tools shock and flame travel together, as they must in a detonation.
A weakness of the case, found with gpucfd: with 4000 cells or more, no detonation starts. The hot layer is too weak, and coarse cells had helped it.

accuracy.note: Each number is how far the computed value is from the theory, on 3200 cells of 0.0375 mm, the finest grid of OpenFOAM's study. Zero would be a perfect match. The first two rows are the problem's requirements.

speed.title: Speed
head: Run
OpenFOAM
gpucfd
rows: the 1200-cell tube in 1024 rows, a full GPU (4383 steps)
speed.note: Most of the time is chemistry: on one core about 150 microseconds for each burnt cell, five times in every time step, against under 3 for the flow. Over a full run the flow takes 2 to 9 % of the processor time. Eight cores were only about twice as fast as one. A single row of cells leaves the GPU almost idle, so gpucfd's times here understate it. gpucfd's times run from creating the solver to the final field; starting the GPU library adds 0.30 s once.
